lead: A defibrillator pushes up to 5000 V across the chest while the ECG electrodes are still stuck on it, so the ECG amplifier needs a protection network that swallows the shock and then recovers. Separately, some arrhythmias come from one small patch of heart muscle, and a cardiac ablation catheter burns that patch with radio-frequency (RF) current delivered through a 4 mm tip electrode. This chapter shows how the protection circuit works, why it protects the amplifier and not the patient, and how the ablation catheter is mapped, powered and kept at a safe tip temperature.
prereq: You need the bio-amplifier and ECG recording, the shock energies from pacemakers and defibrillators, and the current limits from electrical safety.

sections.h3: The problem: a shock arrives at the ECG electrodes

blocks.text: The ECG amplifier reads a signal of about 1 mV at the skin. Its input stage is a low-noise differential amplifier built from devices that tolerate a few volts at most. A defibrillator delivers 200 J to 360 J through paddles on the chest, with a peak voltage of up to about 5000 V. The paddles sit on the same chest as the ECG electrodes, so a large part of that voltage appears across the electrode leads and reaches the amplifier input.

Without protection the amplifier dies in one shock. The input devices break down, a track may fuse, and the monitor is lost for the rest of the arrest — exactly when the team needs to see the rhythm. The protection network sits between the electrodes and the amplifier and does three jobs in order: it limits the current, shunts the excess to a common point, and clamps whatever is left to the supply rails.

The network protects the amplifier, not the patient. The patient is protected by placing the paddles well away from the electrodes, by good electrode contact, and by the current-limiting design of defibrillator-proof leads. Mixing up these two protections is a standard exam error.

items: Series resistor at each electrode. Each lead carries a resistor of tens of kilo-ohms. With 5000 V across the pair, this resistor alone limits the lead current to a fraction of an ampere — for example 5000 V ÷ 40 kΩ = 125 mA with 20 kΩ in each of two leads — instead of amperes.

Neon lamp or spark gap across the inputs. At normal ECG voltages the neon lamp is an open circuit. When the voltage across the neon lamp reaches about 60–100 V (a few hundred volts if the shunt is a spark gap), the gas ionises and the lamp fires, becoming a low-resistance shunt that carries the shock current. In this circuit the lamp is a shunt, not a pilot light.

Clamp diodes at the amplifier input. One diode per input goes to the positive supply and one to the negative supply. Any leftover voltage beyond the rails turns a diode on and is diverted to the supply.

Recovery. After the shock the amplifier is saturated and the lamp is still ionised, so the trace sits off-scale. The channel takes a fraction of a second to a few seconds to settle and show a clean ECG again.

Defibrillator-proof leads carry the series resistors inside the lead or its connector, so the current is limited before it travels down the lead. The shunt and clamp diodes are in the monitor's input circuit, so the protection only works when such a lead is used with a monitor built for it.
Every extra component adds noise and leakage current, so the designer keeps the protection as small as the shock voltage allows.
Screened leads reduce the 50 Hz pickup that the series resistors would otherwise make worse.

sections.h3: Cardiac ablation: burning the faulty patch

blocks.text: Some arrhythmias come from one small region of muscle — an extra pathway between atrium and ventricle, a slow pathway near the AV node, or a focus firing inside a pulmonary vein. Drugs may fail or be needed lifelong. Ablation destroys that few-millimetre patch on purpose, so the abnormal circuit cannot conduct.

items: Mapping. Catheters are passed through a vein to the heart and local electrical signals are recorded to locate the focus. The same catheters pace the heart to test the circuit.
Positioning. A steerable ablation catheter, with a 4 mm tip electrode, is bent by pull wires at the handle until the tip touches the target under X-ray and signal guidance.

Delivery. An RF generator feeds the tip at about 500 kHz, 20 W to 50 W. Current spreads into the tissue, heats it resistively, and the tip is held at 60 °C to 70 °C by a thermocouple that throttles the generator. The circuit is completed by a large dispersive pad on the patient's back or thigh; current flows from the small tip, through the tissue, to this pad, so the heating is concentrated at the tip.
Check. The lesion is a few millimetres deep. The team retests the circuit; if the arrhythmia can still be started, more lesions are placed.

blocks.text: Cryoablation is the alternative: a balloon or tip cooled by expanding gas freezes the same tissue, which is useful near the AV node because cold injury is partly reversible and the effect can be tested before it is permanent. Complications are serious: perforation of the heart wall leading to tamponade, thromboembolism, damage to the AV node needing a pacemaker, and radiation dose to staff and patient from long screening.

spec.aria: Circuit: two chest electrodes, each through a 20 kilohm series resistor, a neon lamp across the two lines, a clamp diode from one line to the positive rail and from the other to the negative rail, and the ECG amplifier, with the 125 milliampere current limit worked out below.

examples.question: An RF ablation generator delivers 50 W into heart tissue that looks like 100 Ω at the catheter tip, at a frequency of 500 kHz. Find the current and the voltage at the tip, and check the power.
steps: Data: power P = 50 W, tissue impedance R = 100 Ω, frequency f = 500 kHz (not needed for the calculation).
Power and resistance give voltage: P = V² ÷ R, so V = √(P × R) = √(50 × 100) = √5000 = 70.7 V.
Power and resistance give current: P = I² × R, so I = √(P ÷ R) = √(50 ÷ 100) = √0.5 = 0.707 A.
Check: I × V = 0.707 A × 70.7 V = 50 W, which matches the generator setting.

Meaning: 70.7 V at 500 kHz sits at the tip. Ablation RF also reaches the ECG leads as interference. Only a small part of this RF voltage couples into the ECG leads, far below the neon firing voltage, so the shunt stays off; the series resistors with the input capacitance form a low-pass filter, and the amplifier's filters remove the rest of the 500 kHz pickup.
examples.answer: The generator drives 0.707 A at 70.7 V into the tissue, which is the set 50 W.

import math
P = 50
R = 100
I = math.sqrt(P / R)
V = math.sqrt(P * R)
print(round(I, 3))
print(round(V, 1))
print(round(I * V, 1))

traps: Saying the protection circuit protects the patient. It protects the ECG amplifier; the patient is protected by paddle placement and by lead design.
Calling the neon lamp an indicator. In this circuit it is the shunt that fires at roughly 60–100 V and carries the shock current.
Mixing the two voltage levels: an ablation tip runs at about 70 V, a defibrillator at up to 5000 V. Both can meet the same electrode lead.
Writing that ablation kills tissue with a shock. It heats tissue with continuous RF current at about 500 kHz, 20–50 W, holding the tip at 60–70 °C.
Forgetting recovery time. A protected amplifier is still saturated for a moment after the shock, so the first part of the trace is unusable.

quiz.q: Name the three elements of a typical ECG input protection network.
quiz.a: Series resistors at each electrode, a neon lamp or spark gap across the inputs, and clamp diodes to the supply rails at the amplifier input.

quiz.q: Why does the protection network sit between the electrodes and the amplifier rather than inside the amplifier?
quiz.a: The first element must limit current before it reaches any semiconductor. Placing the resistors and shunt at the input connector means the shock is reduced before it travels down the lead and into the amplifier, so the amplifier's own devices never see the full 5000 V.

quiz.q: Why does the monitor trace take a moment to return after a shock even with a working protection circuit?
quiz.a: The shock drives the amplifier into saturation and ionises the neon lamp. Until the lamp de-ionises and the amplifier's coupling capacitors and filters settle, the output stays off-scale. Recovery takes a fraction of a second to a few seconds.

quiz.q: An ablation generator is set to 30 W into a tissue impedance of 120 Ω. Find the tip current and voltage.
A lead has a 20 kΩ series resistor in each of two electrodes. A 4000 V shock appears across the pair. Estimate the current through the leads.
quiz.a: The two resistors are in series with the shock path, so R = 40 kΩ. I = V ÷ R = 4000 ÷ 40 000 = 0.1 A = 100 mA, before the neon lamp fires and shunts most of it.

quiz.q: A patient with an implanted pacemaker needs ablation near the AV node. Why might cryoablation be chosen over RF, and what extra protection is needed?
quiz.a: Cold injury near the AV node can be tested: if conduction is lost the tissue can be allowed to rewarm and recover, so the team can decide before making the lesion permanent. RF heat gives an immediate, permanent lesion. Extra care is needed because the RF current can reach the pacemaker lead, so the implanted device is often reprogrammed and the energy is kept low and applied in short steps.

quiz.q: A monitor shows a flat line for two seconds after every shock, then a normal trace. Is the protection circuit faulty?
quiz.a: Not necessarily. Saturation of the amplifier and ionisation of the neon lamp cause exactly this recovery delay. A fault is more likely if the trace never returns, returns distorted, or if the amplifier fails after one shock — then the series resistors or clamp diodes are suspect.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern labs use contact-force and lesion-index catheters that estimate how deep the burn will go from force, power, time and temperature, and pulsed-field ablation is coming in as a non-thermal option that stuns tissue with short high-voltage pulses. Defibrillator protection has moved into integrated front-end chips with on-chip clamps. Search terms for later: 'electrophysiology mapping system', 'contact force sensing catheter', 'pulsed field ablation', 'ECG front-end ESD and defibrillation protection'.
